newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania vows to speed return of lost Jewish assets.
newsitem.headline: Romania vows to speed return of lost Jewish assets.

text.p: Romania's new centrist leaders have pledged swift action to return assets seized from Jews by wartime fascists and later by Communists, an official leading restitution efforts said on Thursday.
"The present government is very positive in its attitude towards our restitution claims," Naphtali Lavie, vice-chairman of the World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO), told Reuters.

He said the new government had shown more courage than the leftist administration it ousted in elections last November by "taking a decision which may be unpopular among certain groups of the population".
Lavie's remarks followed talks on Wednesday with President Emil Constantinescu and Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea.

The WJRO, an umbrella group of major Jewish organisations and the state of Israel created in 1992, seeks the return of Jewish community assets confiscated by the Nazis or nationalised by Eastern Europe's former communist governments.

The World Jewish Congress, a leading member of the WJRO, has headed efforts to press Swiss authorities for compensation for Holocaust survivors whose pre-war savings were deposited in Swiss bank accounts or looted by the Nazis.

A government official said ministers would begin discussions on Friday on returning five properties. Later they would adopt a law on returning assets which the Communists seized from 18 minority groups before being ousted in 1989.
"A law on restitution of assets seized from all ethnic groups should be completed within two months," said Attila Marko, an official from the government's department for the protection of minorities.
Lost Jewish assets include 295 demolished synagogues and hundreds of expropriated properties -- 165 schools and 31 hospitals as well as ritual baths and homes for the elderly.

Jewish community leaders said the first to be returned included Bucharest's Jewish Theatre, a kindergarten turned into a textile mill in Transylvania, and land in northern Romania where Communists demolished a synagogue and ritual bath.
"Nobody will be evicted because of such action," Lavie said.
Half of Romania's 800,000 Jews perished in Nazi death camps and of those who survived, 320,000 left communist Romania for Israel and elsewhere. Only 14,000 Jews remain, most over 60.
The local Jewish community has said it will use proceeds to support 2,500 elderly Jews who survived deportation to wartime concentration camps.

Lavie said the WJRO would set up a foundation to administer property to be returned. The organisation was talking to governments in other ex-communist states often in little hurry to give back property, he said.

"Others got back some lost assets. In Poland, for instance, churches got back their properties," Lavie said. "But the Jewish community, which used to make up 10 percent of (Poland's) population, hadn't got back anything until now."
